lesson.title: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance: Mendel's Rules Meet the Microscope
lesson.summary: The chromosomal theory of inheritance states that genes are located on chromosomes, and that the behavior of chromosomes during meiosis explains the patterns of inheritance Mendel had already worked out mathematically decades earlier without knowing chromosomes existed.
lesson.body:
Gregor Mendel worked out his rules of inheritance in the 1860s purely from the numerical results of pea plant breeding experiments. He had no knowledge of chromosomes or DNA as the physical basis of heredity, since neither had yet been identified as the material responsible for passing traits from parent to offspring. Instead, Mendel inferred the existence of abstract hereditary factors, what we now call genes, that come in pairs, separate during the formation of reproductive cells, and are passed to offspring in predictable ratios. For decades, this remained a mathematical description with no known physical mechanism behind it.

That changed in the early 1900s, when biologists including Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri, working independently, noticed something striking. The behavior of chromosomes during meiosis, in eukaryotic cells, chromosomes exist in homologous pairs, one maternal and one paternal, that pair up and then separate so that each gamete receives just one member of each pair, matched exactly the behavior Mendel had inferred for his hereditary factors decades earlier. This insight, that genes are physically located on chromosomes and that chromosome behavior during meiosis is the actual physical mechanism producing Mendel's inheritance patterns, is known as the chromosomal theory of inheritance, sometimes called the Sutton-Boveri chromosome theory.

The parallels are worth spelling out directly. Mendel's hereditary factors exist in pairs within an individual, one inherited from each parent, and diploid eukaryotic cells likewise carry chromosomes in homologous pairs, one maternal and one paternal. Mendel found that the two factors for a trait separate from each other during the formation of reproductive cells, and this matches exactly how homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis I. Mendel also found that factors for different traits are often inherited independently of one another, which matches how different homologous chromosome pairs orient and separate independently of each other during meiosis I.

This theory is significant because it united two previously separate fields, cytology, the microscope-based study of cell structures such as chromosomes, and genetics, the study of inherited traits, into a single coherent picture. It gave Mendel's abstract hereditary factors a physical, observable home. It also set up an important refinement for later genetics: since each chromosome carries many genes strung along its length, genes on the same chromosome do not always assort independently of one another, they can be linked, which is exactly why crossing over and genetic recombination, covered earlier, matter so much for shuffling those linked genes apart. With this physical foundation in place, the next chapters turn to Mendel's actual laws themselves, starting with the law of segregation.
